html: The Wayana are a Carib-speaking people of the south-eastern Guiana highlands, on the upper Maroni (Lawa) River and its tributaries, in a region split between Suriname, French Guiana and Brazil. In 1980 they numbered about 1,500. They live in riverside villages, growing cassava, fishing and hunting, and are known for the maraké, a coming-of-age ordeal of wasp and ant stings, and for painted roof discs in their round houses. In Brazil they live together with the Aparai. Since the 1990s mercury from illegal gold mining has poisoned their rivers. Their neighbours include the Tiriyó.
